# Abandoning bloodletting, purging and mercury (end of humoral medicine) (`bloodletting_harm`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/medicine.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Medicine & hygiene (`medicine`)
- Deps: helped by controlled_trial, empiricism_over_authority, blood_circulation, placebo_blinding
- Core idea: The standard treatments of learned medicine from Galen to the 1850s (opening a vein, purging, forced vomiting, blistering, mercury salts) rest on the theory of four humours and weaken the patient; in fevers, diarrhoea, childbirth and after wounds they kill. A sick person needs rest, water, food, warmth and cleanliness. The treatments seemed to work because most illnesses get better by themselves and the doctor took the credit. In Paris, Pierre Louis compared pneumonia patients bled early with those bled later. Mortality was higher in the early group, but the groups differed in age and had been selected by the course of their illness.
- Pitfalls:
  - Attacking the physicians head-on without numbers; they have 1,500 years of authority and the patient's own expectations on their side
  - Throwing out the remedies that do work with the theory: opium, cinchona bark, willow bark, setting bones, lancing abscesses
  - Replacing bleeding with another untested cure of one's own
  - Thinking only Europe did this: bloodletting and purging were also standard in Indian, Islamic and Mesoamerican medicine
- History: greece: c. 400 BC – Hippocratic writings; humoral theory with a cautious, mostly dietary therapy; rome: 2nd c. AD – Galen makes bloodletting a universal remedy; india: early centuries AD – Sushruta Samhita describes venesection and leeches (dating of the text disputed); islamic: 9th–11th c. – venesection (fasd) and cupping (hijama) systematised by al-Razi and Ibn Sina; europe: 1648 – van Helmont proposes a trial by lot of bleeding against no bleeding (never held); 1799 George Washington dies after losing about 2.4 litres of blood in a day; 1835 Pierre Louis's numerical method shows little benefit; abandoned c. 1850–1900
- Read:
  - Pierre-Charles-Alexandre Louis, Recherches sur les effets de la saignée dans quelques maladies inflammatoires (1835)
  - David Wootton, Bad Medicine: Doctors Doing Harm Since Hippocrates (2006)
